name: Fable Barbell
strategy: Risk-balanced barbell for an AI-led drawdown with the ten-year back above 5% and crude down to the low $80s: an 11% aggressive sleeve (AVGO plus a small QQQ rebuild after the NVDA stop) re-stopped from the new fill, against 36% rate-resilient ballast (Berkshire, health care, staples, pharma) with energy dropped because its oil premise broke, and 53% cash yielding 4%.
reassessment_note: Research this week (news search and article fetches; I could not pull a price feed, so levels come from my packet and press reports, and I found no close report for Friday 11-20 itself). Three things changed. First, the energy leg's premise is gone: the book was built with WTI near $103, and WTI settled about $83 on 11-18/19, the lowest since late August, on a US inventory build and an IEA call for a Q4 surplus. XLE is down 10.0% from my fill and 2 points from its stop; I would rather exit on a broken thesis than wait for the stop to do it. Second, the AI sell-off is no longer just a rates story: press reports cite bubble worries, post-midterm regulation risk, and the sudden resignation of Nvidia's CEO on 11-19, with the S&P 500 down six sessions running into Thursday and over 90% of constituents falling. My NVDA leg already stopped out on 11-10, so the aggressive end is down to 6% AVGO. A barbell with almost nothing at the aggressive end is not a barbell, but the ten-year is back at about 5.04% and a December hike is still live, so I rebuild only slightly and through the index rather than a single name carrying CEO-succession risk. Third, the ballast worked: the book is -0.5% since inception versus SPY -7.9%, so I keep it and move a little of the freed energy weight into staples and JNJ, the two legs that held flat through the week. Net effect: gross falls from 58% as registered to 47%, cash rises to 53%.

positions.thesis: Kept at 6% as the single-name half of the aggressive sleeve. It is down only 5.5% from my 11-02 fill through an AI wipe-out that stopped NVDA at -16%, and its custom-accelerator and networking revenue is contracted with hyperscalers rather than tied to Nvidia's leadership question. Size stays small because rates near 5% are the stated reason AI capex funding is being doubted; the 15% stop is taken from the new fill.

A small rebuild of the aggressive end after the NVDA stop. The Nasdaq is roughly 12% or more off its October record after six-plus straight losses, which is where a reflex bounce becomes likely, but I do not want that bet resting on one company the week its CEO resigned. An index leg gives growth beta with the single-name risk diluted. 5% with a 10% stop caps the damage at about half a point of NAV if the slide continues.

The core of the ballast and the only leg up from its fill (+2.5%) during an 8% market drop. A very large cash and T-bill pile earns more as short rates rise, and the insurance and rail earnings are not an AI-capex story. Kept at the largest weight; a 15% stop is added because this week showed that correlations can jump.

Health care fell about 4% from my fill against roughly 8-9% for the index, so it cushioned but did not protect. Kept at 6% rather than raised: demand is insensitive to rates and to AI spending, but the sector has not been immune to forced selling.

Staples were essentially flat from my fill (-0.4%) through the worst week of the book's life, the cleanest ballast behaviour I hold. Raised from 5% to 6% with part of the freed energy weight; lower crude also eases input and freight costs for the group.
Flat from its fill (-0.03%) while the market fell 8%. AAA-rated balance sheet, no dependence on capital markets with the ten-year at 5%. Raised from 4% to 5%; a 15% stop added.

The weak ballast leg at -9.9% from its fill, and I did not find company-specific news that explains it, which I state plainly. Kept at 4% and not added to: the valuation is low and the cash flows are not rate-sensitive, but it has behaved like a risk asset, so it now carries a 12% stop from the new fill instead of none.
